clue.text: Pop cuddling mom with both hands entwined? That's rather fruity!

definitions.note: a noun-phrase definition: something with a strong fruit flavour

indicators.note: to cuddle is to hold in your arms, so the drink wraps round the other letters

parts.note: pop is a fizzy soft drink, and orangeade is one

indicators.note: things entwined are twisted together, so these letters are mixed up

parts.note: mama is an informal word for a mother
R and L are the abbreviations for right and left

explanation.surface: A soft drink served while hugging Mum, hand in hand, makes a rather fruity treat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop' looks like a father but is a fizzy drink; 'entwined' mixes the mother's name with the two hands to give MARMAL, held by 'cuddling'.
explanation.definitionFit: This breakfast preserve made from citrus peel is strongly flavoured with fruit.

clue.text: British involved in stirring up EU malice? No, no, no … hardly ever

indicators.note: to be involved in something is to be inside it, so this letter goes into the mixture
stirring up a pot mixes its contents, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone refuses three times to stir up European ill feeling, saying it rarely happens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stirring up' rearranges EUMALICE plus NONONO, and 'involved in' slips B among them.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for something occurring very rarely, as seldom as a second full moon in a calendar month.

clue.text: Something similar to 21 put into cheap ricotta

indicators.note: the answer has been put into the run of letters of the next two words

explanation.surface: A recipe note: something rather like a soft fruit added to a cheap tub of ricotta.
explanation.walkthrough: 21 is 21-down, PEACH; the answer is a close cousin of that fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: An orange stone fruit closely related to, and much like, the downy fruit at 21.

clue.text: Learner's environmentally friendly instrument

parts.note: green describes things kind to the environment
a horn is a brass musical instrument

explanation.surface: A student owns an eco-friendly musical instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: A novice or raw beginner, someone still inexperienced and learning the ropes.

clue.text: Concept car test turning Grand Prix on its head

parts.note: the MOT is the annual roadworthiness test for British cars

indicators.note: turning here means flipping the racing letters over, read in reverse
on its head completes the image: in a down clue the letters are read upside down, i.e. backwards

parts.note: Grand Prix racing is Formula One, F1, with the 1 read as I

explanation.surface: A concept car being tested by flipping a racing car upside down.
explanation.walkthrough: MOT is Britain's annual roadworthiness test for vehicles. 'turning on its head' turns F1 into IF.
explanation.definitionFit: A motif is a recurring idea or theme running through a work.

clue.text: One looking green about the gills? Quite the opposite!

definitions.text: One looking green about the gills? Quite the opposite!

parts.words: One looking green about the gills? Quite the opposite!
parts.note: green about the gills means looking sick; the opposite of green is red, and this creature literally has gills

explanation.surface: Someone looks queasy, but apparently it is the very reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'gills' literally: a fish with gills, coloured red rather than green.
explanation.definitionFit: A reddish sea fish prized in Mediterranean cooking, which breathes through gills.

clue.text: Cash found in grandma's settee

indicators.note: the answer is found in the run of letters across these words

explanation.surface: Money discovered down the back of Granny's sofa.
explanation.definitionFit: Cash counts as a resource of value, a thing a business owns on its balance sheet.

clue.text: Vessel from which a pack animal is injected with polonium

indicators.note: being injected puts something inside, so the element's symbol goes into the animal

parts.note: a mule is a beast of burden used for carrying loads
Po is the chemical symbol for polonium

explanation.surface: A sinister scene: a vial used to inject a beast of burden with a radioactive poison.
explanation.definitionFit: A small sealed glass container holding a dose of medicine for injection.

clue.text: In West Germany, he got drunk (he adored Margaux)

indicators.note: getting drunk leaves you scrambled, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A man in West Germany got drunk, partial to a fine claret from Margaux.
explanation.walkthrough: The American novelist loved wine, and his granddaughter Margaux was reportedly named after the Bordeaux wine; the drinking surface fits his reputation.
explanation.definitionFit: The hard-drinking American author was famously fond of the Bordeaux wine Château Margaux.

clue.text: Mark — my vicar — leaving Oregon

parts.note: cor is a British exclamation of surprise, like 'my!'

indicators.note: leaving means going out of, so these letters drop out

parts.note: a rector is a parish priest, like a vicar
OR is the postal abbreviation for Oregon

explanation.surface: Someone named Mark, a vicar, departing from the state of Oregon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark' looks like a man's name but is the verb, as a teacher marks work.
explanation.definitionFit: To mark homework is to put it right, indicating the errors.

clue.text: Collector of rubbish Dutch puns at work

indicators.note: letters put to work are worked into a new order

explanation.surface: Dutch wordplay dismissed as rubbish while the punsters are busy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at work' reads as one phrase, but the 'at' is part of the anagram letters, rearranged to USTPAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A flat scoop into which floor sweepings are brushed, gathering up dirt.

clue.text: From old Peru, visiting US lavatory

parts.note: someone visiting a place is in it
can is American slang for a toilet

explanation.surface: A traveller from Peru using an American toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: Relating to the ancient empire that ruled the Andes before the Spanish conquest.

clue.text: Smurf going round eating regular chunks of vintage UK sweets

indicators.note: eating takes something in, so the picked letters go inside
going round turns the little blue character's name backwards
regular chunks are evenly spaced letters, here every second one

explanation.surface: A cartoon Smurf spins around munching on old-fashioned British candy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going round' reverses the little blue character; 'regular chunks of' takes every second letter of 'vintage UK', giving ITGU, which 'eating' encloses.
explanation.definitionFit: A brand of chewy fruit-flavoured confectionery sold in Britain.

clue.text: Gold hot new Iranian coin produced by 8?

parts.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold

indicators.note: a new version of the word is a rearranged one

parts.note: the rial is the currency of Iran

explanation.surface: A shiny new Iranian gold coin minted by the person at 8.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' rearranges HOT to THO. 8 is the novelist at 8-down, so his work is that of a writer.
explanation.definitionFit: Anything a writer such as the novelist at 8 produces belongs to the writer, a novelist's output.

clue.text: Quarantine no.1 hit featuring three consecutive notes

indicators.note: a thing featuring something has it within, so the notes sit inside

parts.note: number one is I, the Roman numeral
a hit show is one that is on, running to full houses
so, la and ti are three successive steps of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A top-selling single about quarantine whose melody runs up three neighbouring notes.
explanation.walkthrough: SO, LA and TI are consecutive tonic sol-fa notes; they sit between I and ON.
explanation.definitionFit: Keeping someone apart from others to prevent infection spreading is being kept in seclusion.

clue.text: They're used to biting temperature (the east winds)

indicators.note: something that winds twists about, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Biting temperatures as the east winds blow in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'winds' reads as a noun but is the verb, twisting THE into ETH.
explanation.definitionFit: The hard white structures in the mouth do the chewing and chomping.

clue.text: CEO: the pick of the bunch?

definitions.meaning: the chief executive is the boss, the most important person
the best fruit chosen from a hand of bananas, read literally

explanation.surface: Asking whether the chief executive is the best of the lot.
explanation.definitionFit: A slang term for the boss, and literally the finest fruit in a bunch.

clue.text: French paper putting down Germany and Spain in pithy article

indicators.note: putting down means dropping these letters out

parts.note: Le Monde is a leading French daily newspaper
D is the international vehicle code for Germany
E is the international vehicle code for Spain

explanation.surface: A French newspaper running down two European nations in a terse piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pithy article' suggests concise journalism; read literally, it is a fruit with lots of pith.
explanation.definitionFit: A citrus fruit with a thick layer of white pith beneath its yellow rind.

clue.text: Like Robin's men when they've been at the mead?

definitions.text: Like Robin's men when they've been at the mead?

parts.words: Like Robin's men when they've been at the mead?
parts.note: Robin Hood's band were the Merry Men; after drinking honey wine they would be even jollier

explanation.surface: A picture of Robin Hood's band after a session on the honey wine.
explanation.definitionFit: The comparative of jolly or tipsy: more cheerful, as drinkers become after mead.

clue.text: Superior class functioning brilliantly

parts.note: on top means above or superior
a form is a school class

explanation.surface: A top school class performing excellently.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for performing at one's very best.

clue.text: Old north-eastern football side tabled weakest possible bid

parts.note: NE is the abbreviation for north-east
a football team is a club

explanation.surface: An old football team from the North East made a feeble offer.
explanation.walkthrough: In bridge, bidding starts with one of a suit, and clubs rank lowest, so this is the lowest opening bid.
explanation.definitionFit: In the card game bridge, the lowest-ranking possible opening bid at the table.

clue.text: Super, A-one, amazing people from the continent

indicators.note: amazing suggests being thrown into confusion, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Praise for superb, first-rate visitors from mainland Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the continent' is the British way of referring to mainland Europe.
explanation.definitionFit: Inhabitants of mainland Europe, as Britons call the Continent.

clue.text: Pub stocking chaser, oddly revolting flavour of schnapps

indicators.note: a pub stocking a drink holds it, so these letters go inside

parts.note: PH is the map abbreviation for a public house

indicators.note: revolting means turning over, so the letters run backwards
the odd-numbered letters of the word are taken

explanation.surface: A bar sells a chaser with a nasty schnapps flavour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolting' suggests disgust but means turning over: 'oddly' picks the first, third and fifth letters of 'chaser', reversed to EAC, which 'stocking' holds.
explanation.definitionFit: Peach is a popular fruit flavouring in schnapps liqueurs.

clue.text: Hotel out of Japanese food beginning to exasperate girl

indicators.note: out of here means removed from, so the letter is taken away

parts.note: sushi is Japanese vinegared rice with raw fish
Hotel is H in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: the beginning of the word means its first letter

explanation.surface: A hotel runs out of sushi, which starts to exasperate a young woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Susie is a female first name, as crosswords often use for a lass.

clue.text: Had dinner at home — starter of escabeche (preserved)

indicators.note: something preserved is kept safe inside, so the letter is enclosed

parts.note: in means at home

indicators.note: the starter is the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone dined at home on a starter of escabeche, a pickled fish dish.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition covers 'Had dinner' only, as 'at home' is also part of the wordplay and the answer's IN already carries that sense.
explanation.definitionFit: To eat a meal at your own house rather than going out to dine.

clue.text: Working with paper Boris undressed good friend in Paris

indicators.note: undressed strips off the outer letters, leaving the middle

parts.note: ami is French for friend

explanation.surface: Boris, undressed, doing paperwork with a good friend in Paris.
explanation.definitionFit: The Japanese art of folding paper into decorative shapes.

clue.text: Bird down

definitions.meaning: to down a drink is to gulp it

explanation.definitionFit: A migratory songbird, and also the verb meaning to gulp something down.

clue.text: It followed Emma (3) at baby shower

indicators.note: shower here is a mess or rabble, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the number refers to the answer to 3-down, a novice

explanation.surface: A guest arrives at a baby shower right behind a woman called Emma.
explanation.walkthrough: '(3)' looks like a letter count but points to 3-down's answer, which 'shower' (a rabble) mixes with the next two words. Austen's novel was published after Emma.
explanation.definitionFit: Jane Austen's novel was published in 1817, after her earlier novel Emma of 1815.
